stem:
An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a fall at home. Her daughter reports that her mother has been "not quite right" for two days, sometimes drowsy in the afternoons and then wide awake and confused about who her visitors are at night. She has a background of osteoarthritis and hypertension. She usually manages her own medications and does her own shopping with a taxi.

On assessment she is alert but slow. She names her daughter but says the year is 1998 and cannot name the current Prime Minister or the one before. Asked to state the months of the year backwards from December, she gets to October, then loses the sequence and starts listing days of the week instead. Her daughter confirms she has never been like this at baseline.

data_table.Observations: Pulse 88, BP 142/84 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius.
data_table.Bedside cognition: Alertness: mildly abnormal (drowsy but rousable in prior hour per triage). AMT4: age correct, year 1998 (incorrect), place "the hospital" (correct), DOB correct. Months backwards: 2 errors and abandonment.
data_table.Collateral: Baseline independent, no prior cognitive concerns per GP letter.

lead_in: Which single interpretation of the 4AT screen is correct?

options.text: Score 0 to 3, cognitive impairment unlikely and no further delirium workup indicated today
options.rationale: The abnormal alertness item alone scores 4 on the 4AT and immediately places her in the delirium-possible band; adding the AMT4 error and the months-backwards abandonment takes the total higher, not lower (Source: 4AT scoring guide, ANZSGM endorsed).

options.text: Score 1 to 3, possible cognitive impairment only, arrange outpatient memory clinic referral
options.rationale: A 4AT total in this scenario is at least 4 because the alertness item alone contributes 4 points, which crosses the threshold for possible delirium and requires acute workup rather than outpatient memory referral (Source: 4AT scoring guide).

options.text: Score 4 or above with abnormal alertness, indicating possible delirium and precipitant search
options.rationale: Abnormal alertness scores 4 by itself on the 4AT and reaches the delirium-possible threshold regardless of the other items; the fluctuating course and inattention (months-backwards abandonment) reinforce this and mandate a search for precipitants (Source: ANZSGM Delirium Position Statement; 4AT).

options.text: Score 4 or above but attributable to dementia alone given her age, so no acute precipitant search needed
options.rationale: The collateral confirms she was cognitively independent at baseline two days ago; acute fluctuating change with abnormal alertness in a previously independent older person is delirium until proven otherwise and always earns a precipitant search (Source: ANZSGM Delirium Position Statement).

options.text: Score is uninterpretable without a formal MMSE or MoCA and delirium diagnosis should be deferred
options.rationale: The 4AT is a stand-alone bedside screen designed for exactly this situation and does not require MMSE or MoCA to be scored or acted on; deferral delays reversible-cause identification (Source: 4AT scoring guide).

explanation.summary: The 4AT alertness item scores 0 (normal) or 4 (any clearly abnormal alertness during assessment). A total of 4 or more is the threshold for possible delirium and triggers an acute precipitant search regardless of prior cognitive status. AMT4 errors add 1 point per error and any error on months-backwards or abandonment adds 2 for acute change.
key_points: Alertness item: 0 or 4 (no middle ground)
Total 4 or above equals possible delirium
Fluctuating course plus inattention is the classic delirium signature
Acute change from a documented baseline is not "just dementia"
explanation.pearls: In the older person with acute confusion, the 4AT beats waiting for a formal cognitive test because it is designed to be done in under two minutes at the bedside.

stem:
A 79-year-old man attends the general practice with his wife, who has taken time off work to come with him. Over the last four months he has become withdrawn and stopped attending his weekly bowls club. He complains that his memory is failing and he cannot concentrate on the newspaper. He denies any recent illness, hospital admission, medication change or alcohol use above his usual two beers a week.

On examination he is oriented to person, place and date. He answers questions with "I don't know" repeatedly but on encouragement can register three items and recall two after five minutes. His MoCA score is 22 out of 30. His wife notes that his sleep is fragmented with 3 am wakening and his appetite is poor. Physical examination and screening bloods (FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, calcium) are within normal limits.

data_table.Cognition: Oriented x3. MoCA 22/30 with effort-limited errors in attention and delayed recall.
data_table.Mood/sleep: Fragmented sleep with early morning wakening, appetite reduced, anhedonia and social withdrawal for 4 months.
data_table.Bloods: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, corrected calcium all within normal limits.

lead_in: Which pattern best fits this presentation?

options.text: Acute confusional state with fluctuating attention consistent with hypoactive delirium
options.rationale: Delirium requires acute onset over hours to days with fluctuating course and impaired attention; this is a subacute picture over months with normal orientation and no fluctuation, and the workup shows no reversible precipitant (Source: ANZSGM Delirium Position Statement).

options.text: Late-life depression with cognitive slowing, formerly termed depressive pseudo-dementia
options.rationale: Subacute onset over months, anhedonia, early morning wakening, poor appetite, "I don't know" answers that improve with encouragement, and preserved orientation with only mild MoCA impairment are the classic pseudo-dementia pattern; treating the depression usually restores cognition (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Early Alzheimer's dementia with anosognosia and preserved insight into daily function
options.rationale: Alzheimer's typically presents with insidious short-term memory loss over 12 months or more with LOSS of insight and preserved effort on testing; complaining of memory problems while making effort-limited errors argues against this pattern (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Vascular cognitive impairment based on the stepwise decline and vascular risk profile
options.rationale: There is no history of stepwise decline, no described vascular events, and no vascular risk factors detailed; the trajectory here is a continuous 4-month decline with prominent mood features rather than stepwise cognitive drops (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Frontotemporal dementia behavioural variant given social withdrawal and reduced engagement
options.rationale: Behavioural-variant FTD features disinhibition, apathy without dysphoria, stereotyped behaviours and dietary change with early loss of empathy; this man has classical melancholic mood features rather than the frontal-behavioural syndrome (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

explanation.summary: Late-life depression can mimic dementia (pseudo-dementia) with cognitive slowing, poor concentration, and low MoCA scores. Distinguishing features from true dementia are subacute onset, prominent mood symptoms (early morning wakening, anhedonia, poor appetite), preserved orientation, and effort-limited rather than error-prone cognitive performance. Cognition usually normalises when depression is treated.
key_points: Pseudo-dementia: subacute, mood-driven, effort-limited testing
Dementia: insidious, insight loss, error-prone testing
Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattention core feature
Screen bloods (FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, calcium) mandatory in cognitive workup
explanation.pearls: "I don't know" answers that improve with prompting point to depression; confabulated answers that stay wrong point to dementia.

stem:
An 84-year-old woman on the general medical ward has developed a hypoactive delirium 48 hours after admission for a lower respiratory tract infection now improving on oral amoxicillin. Nursing staff report she is drowsy through the day, minimally engaged at meals, and disoriented to place overnight. She has no fever and vital signs are within normal limits today. Chest X-ray shows improving consolidation.

Her regular medications are shown below. Bloods today: sodium 136 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, calcium and TSH within normal limits, urinalysis clear. She had a normal cognitive assessment on admission and there was no evidence of cerebrovascular event on non-contrast CT head this morning.

data_table.Medications: Oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily (urge incontinence), amitriptyline 25 mg nocte (chronic low back pain), diazepam 5 mg PRN (recently "regular" per nursing observation chart, three doses in 24 h), amoxicillin 500 mg tds, paracetamol 1 g qid, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte.
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145), urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, corrected calcium and TSH within normal limits.
data_table.Imaging: CT head: no acute intracranial pathology. CXR: improving consolidation.

lead_in: Which single medication change is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and reassess cognition in 48 hours as a common contributor to delirium in older adults
options.rationale: Statins are not a recognised anticholinergic contributor to delirium; there are three higher-yield targets already on the chart (Source: STOPP/START criteria; AMH).

options.text: Switch amoxicillin to intravenous ceftriaxone to treat presumed occult meningitis contributing to delirium
options.rationale: There is no fever, no meningism, improving consolidation and no imaging concern; empirical broadening of antibiotics without a source is not the correct move (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Add risperidone 0.5 mg at night with structured behavioural charting to manage the hypoactive delirium symptoms
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not indicated for hypoactive delirium and add anticholinergic and cardiovascular risk; the first move is to remove offending drugs and correct precipitants (Source: ANZSGM Delirium Position Statement; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease amoxicillin now for suspected antibiotic-induced encephalopathy given the temporal association with admission
options.rationale: Amoxicillin encephalopathy is rare, usually seen in severe renal impairment and with beta-lactams like cefepime; her creatinine is normal and the infection is still under treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Cease oxybutynin, amitriptyline and PRN diazepam and use non-pharmacological measures for symptom control
options.rationale: Oxybutynin and amitriptyline both carry high anticholinergic burden and diazepam has a long active metabolite with strong CNS depressant effect in the elderly; each independently precipitates delirium and all three qualify for cessation under STOPP criteria in this setting (Source: STOPP/START criteria; ANZSGM Delirium Position Statement).

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics (oxybutynin, TCAs, older antihistamines) and benzodiazepines (especially long-acting agents like diazepam) are among the highest-yield reversible causes of delirium in hospitalised older adults. STOPP criteria and ANZSGM guidance make medication review the first-line intervention before considering pharmacological treatment of the delirium itself.
key_points: Anticholinergic burden = urgent target in delirium
Diazepam active metabolite half-life over 100 h in elderly
Antipsychotics never for hypoactive delirium
Treat the cause first, symptom management second
explanation.pearls: In a delirious older person, read the medication chart before writing anything new.

stem:
An 86-year-old man on the geriatric medicine ward has been agitated overnight, pulling at his intravenous cannula and attempting to climb over the cot sides despite one-to-one nursing. He was admitted 48 hours ago with a urinary tract infection and is on ceftriaxone. His delirium workup has identified the UTI as the precipitant; a repeat CT head this morning showed no new pathology. Non-pharmacological measures (reorientation, family at bedside, quiet single room, hearing aids in) have not settled him.

He now poses a risk of falling and of self-extubating the cannula. He is haemodynamically stable. His medications include cefriaxone, paracetamol, and a home dose of atenolol 25 mg daily. He has no known allergies, no history of Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, and a normal QTc of 420 ms on today's ECG.

data_table.Observations: Pulse 92, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius.
data_table.Behaviour: RASS +3, pulling at cannula, attempting to climb, non-verbally responsive to redirection for less than 30 seconds.

lead_in: Which single pharmacological agent and dose is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally, repeated in 30 minutes if agitation not settled
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in older adults and are reserved for alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium; diazepam's long-acting metabolite makes this a particularly poor choice (Source: ANZSGM Delirium Position Statement).

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg orally with a 60-minute review before any repeat dose
options.rationale: When non-pharmacological measures fail and there is imminent risk to self, low-dose haloperidol (0.25 to 0.5 mg orally) is the first-line short-term option in delirium without Lewy body dementia or Parkinson's disease, with strict low-dose starting and interval-based review (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; ANZSGM).

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg orally as a single sedating dose overnight
options.rationale: Olanzapine 10 mg is a high starting dose in the frail elderly, carries substantial anticholinergic burden and risks over-sedation and postural hypotension; low-dose haloperidol is preferred short-term (Source: AMH: olanzapine).

options.text: Zopiclone 7.5 mg orally to enforce sleep and end the agitation cycle
options.rationale: Z-drugs share the delirium-worsening pharmacology of benzodiazepines and add fall risk in older adults; they are not appropriate for acute delirium agitation (Source: STOPP/START criteria).

options.text: Midazolam 5 mg intramuscularly to achieve rapid tranquillisation
options.rationale: IM midazolam is used for acute behavioural disturbance in psychosis or severe agitation refractory to oral options; it is not first-line in geriatric delirium because of respiratory depression and paradoxical worsening (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Non-pharmacological measures come first in delirium. If they fail and there is imminent risk, low-dose oral haloperidol (0.25 to 0.5 mg) is the AU first-line pharmacological option in delirium not caused by Lewy body dementia, Parkinson's disease, or alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal (where benzodiazepines are indicated). Start low, review at intervals, stop as soon as safe.
key_points: Non-pharmacological measures always first
Low-dose haloperidol first-line for non-Lewy, non-withdrawal delirium
Benzodiazepines only for withdrawal delirium
Review daily and cease as soon as safe
explanation.pearls: Rapid tranquillisation in a frail elder is a last resort - start small, review often, stop early.

stem:
An 81-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease living in a residential aged care facility has become verbally aggressive and physically resistive during personal care over the past three weeks. Staff report he shouts and pushes carers away when they try to shower him in the morning. He is otherwise settled at meals, during activities, and in the evening. The facility GP has been asked to review.

His behaviour chart shows escalation only during morning showers (never at bedtime or during meals). There is no fever, urinalysis is clear, chest is clear, bowels are opening daily, he denies pain on movement and paracetamol given empirically for two days did not change the pattern. His medications are donepezil 10 mg mane and perindopril 4 mg mane. Nursing staff ask you to "prescribe something" for the agitation.

data_table.ABC chart pattern: Antecedent = morning shower initiated by unfamiliar carer. Behaviour = shouting and pushing away, resolved within 5 minutes of stopping. Consequence = shower postponed.
data_table.Screen for reversibles: Afebrile, urinalysis clear, chest clear, bowels regular, empirical paracetamol trial x 48 h with no effect.
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg mane, perindopril 4 mg mane.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily as first-line pharmacological management and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for BPSD with risk of harm to self or others or severe distress AFTER non-pharmacological strategies have been trialled and reversibles excluded, not as a first prescription for care-time resistance (Source: RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe lorazepam 0.5 mg orally 30 minutes before each morning shower as pre-emptive sedation
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen cognition, increase fall risk, and are not recommended as first-line for BPSD; scheduling a sedative before a care task also does not address the trigger (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Implement a person-centred care plan tailored to the shower task and review in two weeks
options.rationale: BPSD triggered by a specific care task without evidence of a reversible medical cause is a textbook indication for a person-centred non-pharmacological intervention as the first step; antipsychotics are reserved for risk-of-harm or severe distress after this fails (Source: RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines; Dementia Australia).

options.text: Prescribe quetiapine 25 mg at night to cover both nocturnal agitation risk and residual morning behaviours
options.rationale: The behaviour is confined to morning care and does not occur at night; prescribing a night-time antipsychotic does not target the actual trigger (Source: RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines).

options.text: Cease donepezil as a suspected contributor to the recent behavioural escalation and reassess in four weeks
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not established precipitants of aggression during personal care and abrupt cessation risks cognitive worsening; agitation is not an indication to stop donepezil (Source: AMH: donepezil).

explanation.summary: BPSD management follows a stepwise algorithm. Reversible causes (pain, infection, constipation, urinary retention, medication) are excluded first. Non-pharmacological, person-centred strategies matched to the identified trigger are always the next step. Antipsychotics are reserved for risk-of-harm or severe distress and require a specific target symptom, dose cap, and 6 to 12 week review.
key_points: Exclude reversibles first (DELIRIUM screen)
Person-centred non-pharmacological second
Antipsychotics only if risk of harm or severe distress
ABC charting identifies specific triggers
explanation.pearls: Care-task resistance in dementia is often a communication problem the resident cannot articulate; change the task before changing the drug chart.

stem:
An 83-year-old woman with moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease has escalating aggression over eight weeks in her residential aged care facility, with three incidents of striking staff during personal care and one incident of hitting another resident. A structured non-pharmacological care plan has been in place for six weeks including trigger-avoidance, one-to-one carer during high-risk times, music therapy and pain review. Reversible causes have been excluded (afebrile, urinalysis clear, no constipation, no undiagnosed pain, medications rationalised).

Her daughter, who is the substitute decision maker, has given informed consent to a trial of an antipsychotic after a discussion of risks including stroke, mortality and sedation. She weighs 58 kg, has an eGFR of 62 mL/min/1.73 m2, has no history of Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia, no diabetes, and a QTc of 430 ms on ECG this week.

data_table.Behaviour: Aggression during personal care and one peer-directed episode. Structured non-pharmacological plan for 6 weeks, insufficient effect.
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, urinalysis clear, bowels regular, structured pain assessment negative. ECG QTc 430 ms.
data_table.Baseline: Weight 58 kg, eGFR 62, no diabetes, no PD or DLB.

lead_in: Which prescribing plan best matches Australian guidance?

options.text: Haloperidol 1 mg twice daily orally for the aggression, review at 12 weeks
options.rationale: Haloperidol carries a higher extrapyramidal burden in dementia and is reserved for short-term delirium agitation rather than chronic BPSD management; it is not first-line for aggression in Alzheimer's dementia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Risperidone 2 mg twice daily to achieve rapid effect and review at 6 months
options.rationale: The AU maximum in BPSD is 2 mg daily total, not 2 mg twice daily; a 6-month interval before review far exceeds the recommended 6 to 12 week window and exposes the patient to cumulative cerebrovascular and mortality risk (Source: AMH: risperidone).

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg at night for the same indication, review at 12 weeks
options.rationale: Olanzapine is not the AU first-line antipsychotic for BPSD and 10 mg is a high starting dose in the frail elderly with substantial anticholinergic and metabolic burden (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily with formal review at 6 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic PBS-listed for BPSD in Australia, with a starting dose of 0.25 mg twice daily, a maximum of 2 mg daily in moderate to severe Alzheimer's-related aggression, and a formal 6 to 12 week review because efficacy plateaus early and cerebrovascular and mortality risks accumulate with duration (Source: PBS/RPBS Risperidone BPSD listing; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg at night as a lower-risk alternative, review at 6 weeks
options.rationale: Long-acting benzodiazepines worsen cognition, increase falls and are on STOPP for older adults; they are not an appropriate alternative to risperidone in BPSD (Source: STOPP/START criteria).

explanation.summary: In Australia risperidone is the only antipsychotic PBS-listed for BPSD (moderate to severe Alzheimer's-related aggression when non-pharmacological measures fail). Start 0.25 mg twice daily, titrate cautiously to a maximum of 2 mg daily, and formally review at 6 to 12 weeks. Cerebrovascular and mortality signal drives the mandatory time-limited trial.
key_points: Risperidone is the PBS-listed BPSD antipsychotic
Start 0.25 mg BD, max 2 mg daily total
Review at 6 to 12 weeks and cease or reassess
Consent covers stroke, mortality and sedation
explanation.pearls: The PBS listing is the discipline behind BPSD antipsychotic prescribing - it forces the time-limited, dose-capped trial that stops indefinite drift.

stem:
A 78-year-old man is referred to the emergency department by his GP with escalating visual hallucinations of small animals and children in his lounge room for four weeks, unchanged by reassurance. His wife reports fluctuating cognition day to day, with periods of clarity and periods of "staring into space" for several minutes. She has also noticed a recent tremor and small shuffling steps.

On examination he is oriented but slow, has a symmetric rest tremor in both hands, mild cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, and a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing. There is no fever, no infection screen positive, medications reconciled with no new agents, and imaging shows generalised atrophy without acute pathology. The ED registrar plans to write up an antipsychotic for the hallucinations before discharge to the geriatric medicine ward.

data_table.Motor exam: Symmetric rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity both wrists, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing, expressionless face.
data_table.Cognition: Fluctuating, MoCA 22/30 today with prior GP MoCA 27/30 two weeks ago.
data_table.Precipitant screen: Afebrile, MSU negative, chest clear, no new medications, CT head atrophy only.

lead_in: Which single management step is most appropriate?

options.text: Prescribe haloperidol 0.5 mg orally at night for the hallucinations
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics like haloperidol are contraindicated in dementia with Lewy bodies because of severe antipsychotic sensitivity that can cause life-threatening extrapyramidal reactions and autonomic instability (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily as the PBS-listed BPSD antipsychotic
options.rationale: The PBS BPSD listing for risperidone is specifically for Alzheimer's-related aggression, not for DLB; risperidone carries the same antipsychotic-sensitivity risk in DLB as other agents with strong D2 blockade (Source: PBS/RPBS Risperidone BPSD listing; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Withhold antipsychotics and commence rivastigmine for the neuropsychiatric symptoms
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine has the best evidence in DLB) improve cognition and often reduce visual hallucinations and fluctuations, avoiding the severe antipsychotic-sensitivity risk of D2-blocking agents in DLB (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Prescribe olanzapine 5 mg at night to cover both hallucinations and sleep
options.rationale: Olanzapine has significant D2 blockade and worsens parkinsonism and cognition in DLB; it is not the appropriate agent even when sedation is desired (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Start levodopa/carbidopa to treat the parkinsonism as first priority
options.rationale: Levodopa can worsen hallucinations in DLB and is used cautiously and only after cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms are addressed; it is not the first step in a patient presenting primarily with hallucinations (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder. Severe antipsychotic sensitivity means D2-blocking agents (haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine) can cause life-threatening reactions. Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine best evidence) are first-line; if an antipsychotic is essential, quetiapine at very low dose is the least worst option and must be started with caution.
key_points: DLB core: fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism, RBD
Antipsychotic sensitivity is life-threatening in DLB
Rivastigmine first-line for cognition and hallucinations
If antipsychotic essential: quetiapine, very low dose, cautious
explanation.pearls: Well-formed visual hallucinations plus parkinsonism plus fluctuation should stop your hand before you write haloperidol.

subtopic_detail: Behavioural variant recognition and cholinesterase eligibility
stem:
A 62-year-old man is brought to the memory clinic by his wife of 30 years. Over 18 months he has become disinhibited, making inappropriate sexual comments at his adult daughter's workplace Christmas party and repeatedly walking out of a restaurant without paying. His wife says he has become "flat" and no longer greets her or the grandchildren. He eats large quantities of sweet food and has gained 8 kg.

On cognitive testing his short-term recall is preserved (three items at five minutes). His MoCA is 25 out of 30 with losses on abstraction and verbal fluency. Neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable. MRI brain shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, greater on the right. His son asks whether donepezil, which helped his aunt, might help his father.

data_table.Behavioural change: Disinhibition, apathy, stereotyped eating (sweet foods), loss of empathy, over 18 months.
data_table.Cognition: 3-item recall preserved. MoCA 25/30. Losses on abstraction and verbal fluency.
data_table.MRI brain: Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, right greater than left.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding cholinesterase inhibitor therapy?

options.text: Commence donepezil as the presentation and imaging support behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not effective in behavioural-variant FTD and can worsen behavioural symptoms; the PBS listing for donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine applies to mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia, not FTD (Source: PBS Anti-dementia listing; RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Do not commence cholinesterase inhibitors as the picture supports behavioural-variant FTD
options.rationale: Behavioural-variant FTD (disinhibition, apathy, hyperorality, loss of empathy with preserved short-term memory and frontotemporal atrophy on imaging) does not respond to cholinesterase inhibitors and the PBS listing excludes this indication; management is behavioural and supportive with SSRI trials for specific target symptoms if needed (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia; PBS Anti-dementia listing).

options.text: Commence memantine as the first-line agent because it is licensed for all types of dementia
options.rationale: Memantine is PBS-listed for moderate to severe Alzheimer's dementia only and does not have an evidence base or listing in FTD (Source: PBS Anti-dementia listing).

options.text: Refer directly to neurosurgery for consideration of decompressive surgery
options.rationale: There is no neurosurgical indication in neurodegenerative frontotemporal atrophy; imaging shows atrophy, not a space-occupying process (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Commence risperidone for the behavioural changes without further assessment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for risk-of-harm situations in dementia and are not the first-line management of FTD behavioural change; SSRIs have a better evidence base for specific target symptoms and non-pharmacological measures come first (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

explanation.summary: Behavioural-variant FTD presents in the 50s to 60s with disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, hyperorality and stereotyped behaviours, with preserved short-term memory and frontotemporal atrophy on MRI. Unlike Alzheimer's, cholinesterase inhibitors are ineffective and can worsen behaviour; the AU PBS listing for cholinesterase inhibitors covers mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia specifically. Management is behavioural and supportive; SSRIs may help specific target symptoms.
key_points: bvFTD: disinhibition, apathy, hyperorality, preserved memory
Cholinesterase inhibitors: PBS-listed for mild to moderate AD only
Memantine: moderate to severe AD only
SSRIs for target behavioural symptoms in FTD
explanation.pearls: Preserved short-term memory with prominent behavioural change and frontal-anterior temporal atrophy is FTD until proven otherwise - and the memory drugs will not help.

stem:
A 77-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2), hypertension on perindopril, osteoarthritis and mild urge incontinence presents with a 12-week history of low mood, anhedonia, early morning wakening at 4 am, poor appetite with 4 kg weight loss and passive suicidal ideation without plan. Her PHQ-9 score is 18. She has never taken an antidepressant.

A structured assessment excludes bipolar history, substance use, hypothyroidism (TSH normal), B12 deficiency and abnormal calcium. She lives alone but has daily contact with her daughter. She is worried about "tablets clashing" with her other medications and dislikes side effects. Her current medications are perindopril, atorvastatin, alendronate weekly, and paracetamol PRN.

data_table.Bloods: eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, corrected calcium within normal limits.
data_table.Screening: PHQ-9 18/27, MoCA 27/30, no history of mania or hypomania.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg daily titrated slowly with early sodium check
options.rationale: Sertraline is a preferred first-line SSRI in older adults because of a favourable interaction profile and mid-range half-life; starting low and going slow with an early sodium check addresses the SIADH risk that is highest in the first weeks of therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH: sertraline).

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg at night, titrated for mood and sleep
options.rationale: TCAs carry high anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and cardiac toxicity risk in the elderly and are on STOPP; they are not first-line for late-life depression (Source: STOPP/START criteria; AMH: amitriptyline).

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg daily, chosen for its short elimination half-life
options.rationale: Paroxetine has the highest anticholinergic burden among the SSRIs, prominent discontinuation syndrome and is not preferred in older adults (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, chosen for its once-weekly formulation option
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has an active metabolite with a very long half-life, complicating dose adjustment and switching in older adults; it is not preferred first-line despite adherence benefits (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg daily as an SNRI with dual serotonergic action
options.rationale: Venlafaxine can raise blood pressure at higher doses, has a discontinuation syndrome and SIADH risk similar to SSRIs; it is not preferred as first-line over sertraline in an older adult with hypertension and CKD (Source: AMH: venlafaxine).

explanation.summary: Preferred first-line antidepressants in older adults are sertraline, escitalopram (with dose cap 10 mg in over-65s due to QT signal) and mirtazapine (particularly if insomnia or poor appetite). TCAs and paroxetine are avoided because of anticholinergic burden. All serotonergic agents carry SIADH risk, which is highest in the first 2 to 4 weeks and warrants an early sodium check.
key_points: First-line: sertraline, escitalopram (10 mg cap over 65), mirtazapine
Avoid: TCAs (anticholinergic, cardiac), paroxetine (anticholinergic)
SIADH risk highest first 2 to 4 weeks
Start low, go slow, review at 2 to 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: "Start low, go slow, but do not go so slow you never get there" - undertreatment of late-life depression is common and dangerous.

stem:
A 76-year-old man was started on sertraline 25 mg daily for major depressive disorder three weeks ago, titrated to 50 mg after one week. He now presents to the GP with two days of headache, nausea and unsteadiness. His daughter says he has been slower and has been repeating himself over the last 48 hours. He is on perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension and has no history of heart failure, cirrhosis or thiazide use.

On examination he is euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, JVP not raised, no oedema, and no postural change in blood pressure. Bloods today: sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, cortisol and TSH within normal limits. Urine sodium is 62 mmol/L and urine osmolality is 480 mosmol/kg.

data_table.Serum: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1, urea 4.8, creatinine 82 micromol/L, glucose 5.2, cortisol and TSH within normal limits.
data_table.Volume status: Euvolaemic, no oedema, no postural BP change.
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg daily (started 3 weeks ago), perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue sertraline unchanged, add fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily to raise sodium
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is used for cerebral salt wasting, not for SSRI-induced SIADH; continuing the driver drug will not correct the underlying process (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease sertraline and admit for cautious fluid restriction with serial sodium checks
options.rationale: The clinical and biochemical picture fits SSRI-induced SIADH (euvolaemia, hyponatraemia, urine osmolality inappropriately high, urine sodium above 40 mmol/L, normal cortisol and TSH); the drug must be ceased and fluid restriction with careful sodium correction (rise no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 h) started to avoid osmotic demyelination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH: sertraline).

options.text: Continue sertraline and give 3% hypertonic saline 500 mL over one hour for rapid correction
options.rationale: Bolus hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) and even then in 100 to 150 mL aliquots; the target correction remains no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease perindopril as the most likely offending cause and continue sertraline
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are not a common cause of SIADH and the timing here strongly implicates the newly started SSRI, which is a well-recognised cause of SIADH in older adults (Source: AMH: sertraline).

options.text: Give 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over one hour and reassess
options.rationale: In SIADH, isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because the retained water outweighs the sodium load; fluid restriction is the mainstay, with hypertonic saline reserved for severe neurological symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: SSRIs are a common cause of SIADH in older adults, with risk highest in the first 2 to 4 weeks. Diagnosis requires euvolaemia, hyponatraemia, urine osmolality inappropriately concentrated (over 100 mosmol/kg with plasma hypotonicity), urine sodium above 40 mmol/L, and exclusion of cortisol and thyroid causes. Management is cessation of the drug and cautious fluid restriction; correction must not exceed 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SSRI SIADH risk highest first 2 to 4 weeks
SIADH: euvolaemia, low serum Na, high urine osm, urine Na over 40
Correction cap: 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 h
Isotonic saline can worsen SIADH
explanation.pearls: A confused elder started on an SSRI in the last month: measure sodium before you measure the MMSE.

stem:
An 80-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder has lost 9 kg over three months and is now refusing to eat or drink. She has developed nihilistic delusions that her internal organs are rotting. She has already had adequate 6-week trials of sertraline (titrated to 200 mg) and mirtazapine (titrated to 45 mg) with negligible response, and augmentation with aripiprazole was ceased at 10 days for akathisia. She is now on the inpatient psychiatry ward under an involuntary treatment order.

Her PHQ-9 was 24 on admission and remains 22 today. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and postural hypotension. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (SSRI-related), urea 9.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and albumin 28 g/L. She has no pacemaker, no recent stroke, no unstable ischaemic heart disease and her most recent ECG showed sinus rhythm with QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Illness: Severe MDD with psychotic features (nihilistic), 3 months, food and fluid refusal, 9 kg weight loss.
data_table.Trials to date: Sertraline 200 mg 6 weeks minimal response; mirtazapine 45 mg 6 weeks minimal response; aripiprazole ceased for akathisia at day 10.
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 128 mmol/L, urea 9.6, creatinine 92, albumin 28 g/L.
data_table.Cardiac: No pacemaker, no recent stroke, ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 440 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Continue current pharmacotherapy for a further 4 to 6 weeks to allow full response
options.rationale: Adequate trials have already been completed; continuing failed pharmacotherapy with active food and fluid refusal in an older adult with hyponatraemia and hypoalbuminaemia is not appropriate (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (phenelzine) after a two-week washout
options.rationale: MAOI trials in a physically compromised, dehydrated older adult with food refusal are not the safest or fastest option; ECT delivers response in days to weeks and is preferred over a washout-plus-MAOI approach in this severity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add lithium augmentation to mirtazapine targeting a level of 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is a reasonable strategy for less severe treatment-resistant depression but response takes weeks, and lithium risks toxicity when the patient is dehydrated with rising urea and known SIADH (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add nortriptyline to mirtazapine as a combination antidepressant strategy
options.rationale: Combining TCAs in a dehydrated older adult with postural hypotension is high-risk and slow-acting; ECT has a faster, safer profile in this severity of illness (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as the treatment of choice in this presentation
options.rationale: Severe treatment-resistant depression with psychotic features, food and fluid refusal, and imminent physical risk in an older adult is a first-line indication for ECT, which has faster response times and higher remission rates than any pharmacological option in this presentation (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders; RANZCP ECT PPG).

explanation.summary: First-line ECT indications include severe depression with psychotic features, food/fluid refusal with medical compromise, high suicide risk, catatonia, and severe treatment-resistant depression. Older adults respond as well as or better than younger patients. Response rates around 70 to 80 percent, and older-adult remission is often faster than pharmacological alternatives.
key_points: First-line ECT: psychotic depression, food/fluid refusal, high risk, catatonia
Older adults have equal or superior response to ECT
Speed of response is the safety argument in medical compromise
Common adverse effects: transient memory disturbance, headache, myalgia
explanation.pearls: In severe depression with food refusal, ECT is not a last resort; it is often the safest first choice.

stem:
A 74-year-old man attends his GP two weeks after his wife of 48 years died. He lives alone in the family home, is retired, and has adult children interstate. He has hypertension, hearing loss, chronic back pain and a background of harmful alcohol use with 40 g of alcohol per day. He states his mood is "about what you'd expect" and denies suicidal ideation on direct questioning.

During the consultation you notice he has lost 3 kg since his last visit, has cancelled his upcoming knee surgery consultation and mentions in passing that he has given his fishing gear to his son "because I don't need it any more". His PHQ-9 is 14 with item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead) answered as "nearly every day". He has a licensed firearm at home.

data_table.Risk factors: Male, 74, recent bereavement, socially isolated, harmful alcohol use, chronic pain, hearing loss, firearm at home, giving away possessions, PHQ-9 item 9 positive daily.
data_table.Physical: Weight loss 3 kg since prior visit, cancelled elective surgery.
data_table.Denial: Denies active suicidal ideation on direct questioning.

lead_in: Which single statement about his suicide risk is correct?

options.text: Older men have the lowest completed suicide rate of any Australian age-sex group
options.rationale: This reverses the epidemiology; AIHW data show older men (particularly men aged 85 and above) have the highest completed suicide rate of any Australian age-sex group despite lower attempt rates (Source: AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring).

options.text: Direct denial of suicidal ideation reliably excludes suicide risk in the elderly
options.rationale: Older adults are less likely to disclose suicidal ideation on direct questioning; behavioural indicators (giving away possessions, cancelling future plans, PHQ-9 item 9 positive) may carry more weight than a single verbal denial (Source: RANZCP: Suicide and self-harm assessment).

options.text: Older Australian men have the highest completed suicide rate and this patient warrants urgent psychiatric input
options.rationale: AIHW data confirm men aged 85 and above have the highest age-specific suicide rate in Australia; this patient adds recent bereavement, isolation, alcohol misuse, chronic pain, disability, weight loss, cancelled plans, giving away possessions, firearm access and PHQ-9 item 9 daily to a highest-risk demographic (Source: AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring; RANZCP).

options.text: Attempt-to-completion ratio in older men is similar to that of adolescent females
options.rationale: Older men have the highest attempt-to-completion ratio in Australia, with methods of higher lethality and lower rescue rates; adolescent females have high attempt rates but much lower completion (Source: AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring).

options.text: A firearm at home does not modify suicide risk in an older man because access does not equate to use
options.rationale: Access to lethal means, particularly firearms, is one of the most modifiable risk factors for completed suicide and means restriction is a specific evidence-based intervention (Source: RANZCP: Suicide and self-harm assessment).

explanation.summary: Older Australian men, particularly those aged 85 and above, have the highest completed suicide rate of any age-sex group. They present with fewer verbal disclosures, higher method lethality and lower rescue rates. Key risk factors are bereavement, isolation, chronic pain and disability, alcohol misuse, cognitive change and access to lethal means. Behavioural indicators (giving away possessions, cancelling plans) carry additional weight when direct questioning is negative.
key_points: Men 85+ = highest AU age-specific suicide rate
Older men: fewer warnings, higher lethality
Modifiable: bereavement support, alcohol Rx, means restriction
PHQ-9 item 9 positive is not to be dismissed
explanation.pearls: In an older man in the weeks after bereavement, a passing comment about "not needing it any more" is a suicide risk assessment starting, not ending.

stem:
A 71-year-old man is admitted with a fractured neck of femur after a mechanical fall at home. On day 2 post-op he becomes tremulous, sweating, and mildly confused. His wife discloses that he has consumed a bottle of red wine each evening for the last 20 years and has not had a drink since admission 40 hours ago. His CIWA-Ar score is 14. He has hypertension on amlodipine, mild CKD (eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2), and no cirrhosis on prior imaging.

He is haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and his post-operative pain is well controlled on paracetamol and low-dose oxycodone. Bloods show normal LFTs, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9, glucose 6.0 mmol/L. He has no history of complicated withdrawal or seizures. The intern asks about the appropriate benzodiazepine choice given his age and renal function.

data_table.Withdrawal: CIWA-Ar 14 (tremor, sweating, mild confusion) at 40 h post last drink.
data_table.Bloods: LFTs within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2.
data_table.History: Bottle of wine daily for 20 years, no prior seizures or DTs, no cirrhosis on prior imaging.

lead_in: Which benzodiazepine and dosing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg every hour by symptom-triggered dosing until CIWA-Ar below 10
options.rationale: Diazepam's active metabolites accumulate substantially in older adults and in even mild renal impairment, risking over-sedation, delirium and falls; a shorter-acting agent is preferred in patients over 65 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; AMH: diazepam).

options.text: Phenobarbitone 130 mg intramuscularly as first-line treatment for withdrawal
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory withdrawal or ICU settings and is not a first-line agent for uncomplicated withdrawal on a general ward (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Chlordiazepoxide 50 mg four times daily for 5 days on a fixed schedule
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting agent with active metabolites and is avoided in older adults; fixed-dose schedules deliver more total benzodiazepine than symptom-triggered protocols and increase adverse effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oxazepam 15 to 30 mg symptom-triggered on CIWA-Ar with regular review
options.rationale: Oxazepam and lorazepam are preferred in older adults, hepatic impairment and renal impairment because they are metabolised by glucuronidation without active metabolites; symptom-triggered dosing guided by CIWA-Ar minimises total exposure and reduces delirium risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Withhold benzodiazepines and manage with hydration and clonidine to avoid delirium risk
options.rationale: Withholding benzodiazepines in established withdrawal risks progression to withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are the mainstay of treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: In alcohol withdrawal in older adults or those with hepatic/renal impairment, oxazepam or lorazepam are preferred over diazepam and chlordiazepoxide because glucuronidation metabolism produces no active metabolites and prevents accumulation. Symptom-triggered dosing guided by CIWA-Ar delivers less total benzodiazepine than fixed-dose schedules and reduces adverse effects. Thiamine 100 mg IV or IM is given before any glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
key_points: Over 65: oxazepam or lorazepam (no active metabolites)
Symptom-triggered dosing beats fixed schedule
Diazepam accumulates in older adults and renal impairment
Thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke's
explanation.pearls: Fluctuating confusion in a post-op elder without an obvious infective cause: ask about alcohol before ordering another septic screen.

stem:
A 78-year-old woman has been on temazepam 20 mg at night for 12 years, first prescribed after her husband died. She lives alone, mobilises with a four-wheel walker and had a fall three weeks ago requiring six stitches to her forehead. Her cognitive assessment today is MoCA 25 out of 30. She tells you she "needs" the temazepam to sleep and has been reluctant to change it. She has no formal diagnosis of insomnia disorder and denies mood or anxiety symptoms today.

Her medications are perindopril 5 mg mane, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte and temazepam 20 mg nocte. Her renal function is normal, LFTs are within normal limits and she has no known contraindication to sleep hygiene measures or short-term CBT-I. She has attended one bereavement counselling session in the past.

data_table.History: Temazepam 20 mg nocte for 12 years, recent fall with stitches, lives alone, MoCA 25/30.
data_table.Screen: No current mood or anxiety diagnosis; sleep-hygiene measures not previously trialled.
data_table.Bloods: eGFR over 60, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to deprescribing?

options.text: Cease temazepam abruptly at the next appointment to avoid further fall risk
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of long-term benzodiazepines risks rebound insomnia, anxiety and (rarely) withdrawal seizures; the AU deprescribing guideline advises a gradual, negotiated taper (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing).

options.text: Switch to zopiclone 7.5 mg at night as a safer alternative for chronic use
options.rationale: Z-drugs share the fall, cognitive impairment and dependence profile of benzodiazepines in older adults and are on STOPP for the same reasons; switching does not address the problem (Source: STOPP/START criteria).

options.text: Continue temazepam indefinitely because 12 years of use makes deprescribing unsafe
options.rationale: Long duration of use is a reason to taper more slowly, not to continue indefinitely; ongoing use in an older adult with a recent fall carries clear net harm (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing).

options.text: Negotiate a gradual dose reduction of 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks with CBT-I
options.rationale: AU deprescribing guidance advises a patient-negotiated taper of about 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks (slower for very long-term users) with non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (sleep hygiene, CBT-I) as replacement, in an older adult with a recent fall on chronic benzodiazepine use (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing).

options.text: Add mirtazapine 30 mg at night to cover sleep and then cease temazepam within one week
options.rationale: Adding a second sedating drug in an older adult with a recent fall increases fall and sedation risk; the recommended pathway is a slow taper of the offending agent alongside non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults increase falls, fractures, cognitive impairment and delirium. Deprescribing pathways are negotiated with the patient, structured as gradual dose reductions (typically 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks, slower for very long-term users) and paired with non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (sleep hygiene, CBT-I, stimulus control). Abrupt cessation risks rebound and seizures.
key_points: Taper 10 to 25% every 2 to 4 weeks, slower for years-long use
Non-pharmacological insomnia strategies replace the drug
Z-drugs are equivalent risk, not an escape
Patient negotiation matters for adherence
explanation.pearls: A fall on temazepam is not a reason to prescribe zopiclone; it is a reason to plan a taper.

stem:
An 82-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 24 out of 30, retains capacity for financial and care decisions on formal assessment last month) attends the general practice with her son. He answers most of your questions on her behalf. She has come in for a repeat prescription and to "sort out the pension". You notice bruising in various stages of healing on her upper arms and a small circular burn on her forearm which she attributes to "being clumsy".

When you ask to see her alone, her son says "she gets confused, I need to stay". Her Medicare card and bank card are held by the son. She lives with him after selling her own home last year, with the proceeds transferred into his name to "help pay the bills". On direct questioning alone, she says she is "fine" but avoids eye contact and asks whether her son is going to be told what she says.

data_table.Cognitive status: MoCA 24/30, retains decision-making capacity on formal assessment 4 weeks ago.
data_table.Injuries: Bruising of upper arms in various stages of healing, small circular burn on forearm.
data_table.Financial: Sold own home in past year, proceeds transferred to son's name. Medicare and bank cards held by son.
data_table.Interaction: Son answers on her behalf, resists private interview.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Confront the son directly in the consultation about the injuries and financial concerns
options.rationale: Direct confrontation of a suspected perpetrator in the presence of the victim risks retaliation, loss of trust and further concealment; the priority is safe private interview and structured response (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

options.text: Report to the police today as mandatory reporting of elder abuse applies in all Australian states
options.rationale: Elder abuse is not covered by a national mandatory reporting law equivalent to child protection; only aged care providers have mandatory reporting duties under the Aged Care Act (SIRS scheme). Community elder abuse response is consent-based when the person has capacity (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

options.text: Refer directly to the public guardian for financial substitute decision-making today
options.rationale: She retains decision-making capacity on formal assessment; a guardianship application without her consent and without capacity loss is inappropriate and paternalistic (Source: Office of the Public Advocate).

options.text: Complete the repeat prescription and address her concerns at the next annual review
options.rationale: Multiple concurrent physical and financial abuse indicators demand action at this visit, not deferral; deferral risks escalation and further injury (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

options.text: Interview her alone and, with her consent, contact the state elder abuse helpline
options.rationale: A capacitous older person with multiple abuse indicators (physical injuries in various stages of healing, financial control, thwarted private communication) requires a private interview to enable disclosure, a structured assessment, and a coordinated response through the state elder abuse helpline; her retained capacity means her consent is paramount and mandatory reporting frameworks differ from child protection (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources; Elder Abuse Action Australia).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

explanation.summary: Elder abuse can be physical, financial, emotional, sexual, neglect or a mix. Warning signs include unexplained injuries in various stages of healing, controlled communication, financial transfers, thwarted private interviews and social isolation. In Australia, community elder abuse response is consent-based when the older person has capacity; mandatory reporting under the Aged Care Act (SIRS) applies to aged care providers, not GPs in the community. Each state has an elder abuse helpline (e.g. 1800 ELDERHelp - 1800 353 374 - national line routes to state services).
key_points: Private interview first, capacity-based response
AU community elder abuse response is consent-based
SIRS mandatory reporting is aged-care-provider specific
State elder abuse helpline is core referral
explanation.pearls: When someone else answers every question and holds the bank card, ask to see the patient alone before you print anything.

sources.label: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic risk decision in vascular dementia with recent stroke
stem:
An 84-year-old man with vascular dementia (MMSE 16) is admitted from a residential aged care facility with escalating aggression: he has struck two staff and another resident in the last week, and non-pharmacological measures over four weeks (structured routine, one-to-one, redirection, tailored music) have failed. A full reversible-cause workup is negative. His MRI three months ago showed multiple bilateral small-vessel infarcts and one small right middle cerebral artery cortical infarct sustained six weeks ago from which he has largely recovered motor function.

He is on aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg and no antipsychotic. His current QTc is 460 ms. His son (substitute decision maker) asks for a plan. He has no history of Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. He weighs 62 kg and eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m2.

data_table.Behaviour: Aggression with harm to staff and resident, 4 weeks of failed non-pharmacological plan, reversible-cause workup negative.
data_table.Cerebrovascular: Multiple bilateral small-vessel infarcts; right MCA cortical infarct 6 weeks ago.
data_table.Cardiac/renal: QTc 460 ms, eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m2, weight 62 kg.
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily with informed consent covering stroke and mortality risk
options.rationale: When non-pharmacological measures have genuinely failed and there is a documented risk of harm to self or others, risperidone remains the AU PBS-listed BPSD antipsychotic option even in vascular dementia; the elevated cerebrovascular and mortality risk (particularly relevant in this patient with recent infarct) must be explicitly addressed in consent, the dose kept minimum-effective, QTc rechecked, and formal review at 6 to 12 weeks planned (Source: PBS/RPBS Risperidone BPSD listing; RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines; TGA cerebrovascular warning).

options.text: Prescribe olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as the safest antipsychotic option given the recent stroke
options.rationale: The cerebrovascular signal is a class effect for both risperidone and olanzapine and olanzapine additionally has substantial anticholinergic burden and metabolic risk; it is not the preferred AU BPSD antipsychotic and is not "safer" post-stroke (Source: TGA antipsychotic cerebrovascular warning; RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe haloperidol 1 mg twice daily as a non-atypical option that carries no cerebrovascular signal
options.rationale: Haloperidol also carries mortality and cerebrovascular event signal in dementia and has a higher extrapyramidal burden; it is not preferred over the AU PBS-listed atypical for chronic BPSD (Source: TGA antipsychotic cerebrovascular warning; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 2 mg twice daily as an antipsychotic alternative to avoid cerebrovascular risk
options.rationale: Diazepam is on STOPP for older adults, worsens cognition, increases fall risk, and does not treat aggression in dementia; substituting it for a needed antipsychotic in a risk-of-harm scenario is not appropriate (Source: STOPP/START criteria).

options.text: Continue non-pharmacological measures for another 12 weeks without any medication change
options.rationale: Four weeks of a structured non-pharmacological plan has already failed and there is active risk of harm to staff and residents; continuing indefinitely without pharmacological input is not consistent with the AU risk-of-harm indication for time-limited antipsychotic use (Source: RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The TGA cerebrovascular warning and increased all-cause mortality signal apply to all antipsychotics in dementia. This does not remove risperidone as an option when non-pharmacological measures have failed and there is risk of harm - it raises the bar for consent (substitute decision maker informed of stroke and mortality risk, particularly relevant with recent infarct), for dose (start 0.25 mg twice daily, minimum-effective titration to a maximum of 2 mg daily), for physiological safety (recheck QTc, review renal function) and for review (6 to 12 weeks with intent to withdraw). The competing pull between "do not prescribe post-stroke" and "must treat imminent risk-of-harm" is what makes this a stop-and-think choice.
key_points: TGA cerebrovascular warning applies to all antipsychotics
Risperidone is the PBS-listed BPSD agent (max 2 mg/day)
Non-atypical alternatives share the risk signal
Consent must explicitly cover stroke and mortality risk
explanation.pearls: In a recent stroke plus dementia plus aggression, the answer is not "avoid antipsychotics" but "use the smallest dose of the best-evidenced agent, with the most explicit consent and the tightest review".
